title: Under the spell of the Magellanic Clouds
caption: The Magellanic Clouds above ALMA antennas, Chajnantor plateau, Chile
celestial: Photograph taken at ALMA, Chajnantor plateau, Chile

recognition.text: ESO Picture of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: The Large and Small Magellanic Clouds glow brightly above the antennas of ALMA, the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array, in this image by ESO Photo Ambassador Christoph Malin. It is a single still frame from one of his carefully made time-lapse videos of the observatory.

The two Magellanic Clouds are nearby irregular dwarf galaxies, easy to see without any telescope from the southern hemisphere. Both circle our own galaxy, and there are signs that close passes near the Milky Way have pulled both of them badly out of shape.

ALMA stands 5000 meters up, on the Chajnantor Plateau. ESO describes it as the world's most powerful telescope for studying the Universe at millimeter and submillimeter wavelengths, light far beyond what the eye can see. At the time this picture was released, construction was still under way, with a total of 66 high-precision antennas planned for the site.

understand.summary: This is a still frame from a time-lapse video at the ALMA site, in visible light. The camera settings and color processing are not published.
understand.eye: The Magellanic Clouds are visible to the naked eye from here, but a camera exposure gathers more light, making them and the surrounding stars look brighter.

explore: Europe, North America and East Asia share ALMA, in cooperation with the Republic of Chile. ESO leads construction and operations for Europe, the National Radio Astronomy Observatory for North America, and the National Astronomical Observatory of Japan for East Asia.
alt: Two glowing patches of light in a starry sky above ALMA antennas.
